nameStory: This shrub gets its common name "linden viburnum" because its heart-shaped leaves look remarkably similar to those of the American linden tree. The word "viburnum" comes from Latin, originally used by ancient Romans to describe flexible twigs that could be woven into baskets. It's also called "linden arrowwood" because Native Americans once used the straight, flexible stems of viburnums to make arrow shafts.
description: Linden viburnum is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall and wide, forming a rounded, dense shape. Originally from eastern Asia, this introduced species has made itself at home in parts of New England with its distinctive heart-shaped leaves and showy clusters of small white flowers in spring. What really makes this shrub stand out are its brilliant red berries (called drupes) that appear in late summer and persist well into fall. The overall appearance is neat and garden-like, which makes sense since it's primarily found as an ornamental plant that has occasionally escaped cultivation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with prominent parallel veins that feel slightly rough and fuzzy underneath, arranged opposite each other on the stem. The leaves have small teeth along the edges and turn yellow to reddish-purple in fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers about 3-5 inches across bloom in late spring, creating a sweet, mild fragrance. Each individual flower is very small but the clusters are showy and attract various pollinators.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Bright red, oval berries about 1/3 inch long appear in dense clusters in late summer and fall. The berries feel firm and have a single flat seed inside, and they often persist after leaves drop.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a dense, rounded shrub with multiple stems from the base. The branching pattern is opposite and the bark on young stems is smooth and grayish-brown.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are small, egg-shaped, and reddish-brown, sitting opposite each other on the stems. The buds have visible scales and help identify the plant when leafless.

habitat: In New England, linden viburnum is most commonly found in suburban and urban areas as an ornamental planting that has occasionally escaped to nearby woodlands and forest edges. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade, though it flowers and fruits best with some direct sunlight. You're most likely to spot it in parks, along roadsides, or at the edges of wooded areas near residential developments.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in early spring, followed by conspicuous flat-topped white flower clusters in late spring that attract bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed with heart-shaped foliage, and small green berries begin developing from the spent flowers by mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: The star season - brilliant red berry clusters ripen and leaves turn yellow to reddish-purple before dropping, leaving the bright berries still clinging to branches.
seasonality.winter: Identifiable by its opposite branching pattern, small reddish-brown buds, and often persistent red berries that provide winter interest and food for birds.

funFact: The bright red berries of linden viburnum are like nature's candy store for birds - over 40 species of birds have been documented eating viburnum berries, and they're so nutritious that some birds will strip an entire shrub clean in just a few days during fall migration!
confusionNotes: With its heart-shaped leaves, linden viburnum might be confused with native American linden trees, but remember the simple trick: "Viburnum's the shrub, linden's the tree." Linden trees grow much taller and have different flowers and fruits, while linden viburnum stays shrub-sized with opposite leaves and red berry clusters.
contextualKnowledge: While many viburnums are native to North America and beloved by wildlife, linden viburnum is actually an introduced species from Asia that's primarily used in landscaping. It's generally well-behaved and not considered invasive, but it's worth noting that native viburnum species like hobblebush or arrowwood would provide even better ecological value for local wildlife.
compareHints: Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods). The combination of heart-shaped leaves and bright red berries in dense clusters makes it quite distinctive from its native cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
